b.bio: Henry Spelman of Congham, Norfolk, graduated from Trinity College, Cambridge in 1583, sat in Parliament for Castle Rising (1593 and 1597–98) and later Worcester (1625), was knighted in 1603, served as High Sheriff of Norfolk in 1604, and settled in London near his friend Sir Robert Cotton in 1612. He is best known as an ecclesiastical historian for his Concilia, a systematic compilation of church councils and documents of Britain, whose first volume appeared in 1639 and second posthumously in 1664. Sources give slightly different birth years (c. 1562 vs. 1564?), but agree he died in London in October 1641 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
b.s: The single short work held here traces the origin of church chants and the liturgical office to apostolic and patristic figures—John the Evangelist for the Gallican office, Mark for unified congregational chanting—and argues against attributing the office to a Briton cleric or to Pelagian influence.

b.bio: Henry Smith, called 'silver-tongued Smith,' was a Puritan preacher of Elizabethan London. Sources give differing birth years: the old Dictionary of National Biography places his birth about 1550 at Withcote, Leicestershire; later accounts say c. 1560. He was admitted to Queen's College, Cambridge but did not matriculate there, then studied at Lincoln College, Oxford (B.A. 1579), and prepared for ministry under Richard Greenham at Dry Drayton. Declining a pastoral charge on scruples about subscription, he served as lecturer at St. Clement Danes from 1587, drawing large crowds. Illness forced him to resign by 1590; he spent his last months revising his sermons for the press and was buried at Husbands Bosworth in 1591.
b.s: The works held here are the sermons that made him one of the most popular preachers of Elizabethan London—practical, exegetical preaching on sin, faith, providence, marriage, usury, and the Lord's Supper, with repeated polemic against the Papists and against usurers.

b.bio: Henry Wharton (9 November 1664 – 5 March 1695) was an English clergyman and historian, son of Edmund Wharton, vicar of Worstead, Norfolk. Educated at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, he served as chaplain to Archbishop William Sancroft, who presented him to the Kentish livings of Sundridge and Chartham. He took the oath to William III and Mary II in 1689. His best-known work is Anglia Sacra (1691), a collection of medieval manuscripts on the English church. The Westminster Abbey inscription gives his death as 5 March 1694 aged 31; the ODNB and other sources give 1695.
b.s: The works held here are his dissertations and historical notices prefixed to Aelfric's writings in Migne's Patrologia Latina, sorting out which Aelfric wrote what and correcting earlier identifications against Ussher, Bale, Spelman, and others.

b.bio: The library holds under this name only a 'Prolegomena' printed in PL 68, a volume of Latin patristic texts. Surviving records do not securely identify its author: they describe two distinct Dutchmen bearing this or a closely similar name. One, Henricus Arntzenius, was baptized at Wezel on 10 March 1665 and buried at Utrecht on 14 February 1728; he studied at Groningen from 1685 and was successively conrector and then rector at Arnhem (rector by 1697) and rector at Utrecht from 1720 (NNBW; Biografisch Portaal). The other, Henricus Johannes Arntzenius, son of the Franeker professor Johann Arntzenius (1702–1759), took a doctorate of laws at Franeker on 13 July 1760, served as rector at Leeuwarden and then Zutphen (from 1763), and became professor of Roman law at Groningen in 1774 (German Wikipedia). Neither source connects either man to a patristic edition, so no career details are asserted here.
b.s: The single work held here is an eight-page 'Prolegomena' prefacing material in PL 68; the author's identity cannot be confirmed from the sources given.

b.bio:
Calixtus II (c. c. 1065–1124) — Guy of Burgundy, son of Count William I of Burgundy, was named Archbishop of Vienne in 1088 and served as papal legate in France under Paschal II. He led the opposition in France to the Privilegium of 1111 by which Paschal yielded to Emperor Henry V, attended the Lateran Synod of 1112, and was elected pope at Cluny on 1 February 1119. His pontificate ended the Investiture Controversy through the Concordat of Worms (1122), and he convened the First Lateran Council in March 1123. Prompted by attacks on Jews, he issued the bull Sicut Judaeis forbidding Christians on pain of excommunication from forcing Jews to convert or harming them.

Henricus IV imperator (1050–1106) — Henry IV, son of Henry III, became king of Germany in 1056 and emperor, ruling until his death in 1106. His reign was dominated by the Investiture Controversy with Pope Gregory VII over control of episcopal appointments, which brought his excommunication and his penance at Canossa in 1077, and later rebellion led by his own son. The works held here are not treatises but acts of government: royal diplomas granting churches privileges, immunities, and rights of abbatial election, and constitutions regulating monasteries.
b.s: The works held here are his letters and privileges — chiefly decretals asserting that violation or contempt of papal privilege incurs excommunication, that interdicts spare infant baptism and deathbed penance, that legitimate petitions must not be delayed, and defending freedom to receive sacraments from any catholic bishop — together with the Concordat of Worms itself, the settlement of the Investiture Controversy with Henry V.

b.bio: Henricus Canisius (Hendrik de Hondt), nephew of Saint Peter Canisius, was born at Nijmegen and studied at Leuven; in 1590 he became professor of canon law at Ingolstadt, where he died on 2 September 1610. Sources disagree on his birth year: the Catholic Encyclopedia and Wikipedia give 1562, while Deutsche Biographie gives about 1557. His major historical work, the Antiquae Lectiones (6 vols., Ingolstadt 1601–1604), collected medieval ecclesiastical monuments; a seventh volume, the Promptuarium Ecclesiasticum, was added in 1608 as a supplement. Basnage later recast it as the Thesaurus Monumentorum ecclesiasticorum et historicorum (7 vols., Antwerp, 1725). He also first edited the chronicles of Victor of Tunnuna and John of Biclar and Paul the Deacon's Historia miscella.
b.s: The works held here are editorial notices from his Antiquae Lectiones, in which he printed medieval texts — including the statutes of Corbie attributed to Adalhard (822) and materials on ancient hymns — arguing that only works of certain authorship belong in such a collection.

w: Critical Inquiry into the Gallican Masses

b.bio: Heinrich Joseph Dominicus Denzinger was born at Liège on 10 October 1819 and died at Würzburg on 19 June 1883. After studies at Würzburg and the German College in Rome, he was ordained priest in 1844 and became professor extraordinary of dogmatic theology at Würzburg in 1848, ordinary professor from 1854 until his death. He was a pioneer of positive theology and historical dogmatic (Dogmengeschichte) in Catholic Germany, carrying forward the methods of Möhler and Döllinger: exact investigation of the historical development of doctrine rather than philosophical speculation. He is best known as author of the Enchiridion symbolorum et definitionum.
b.s: The works held here are his nineteenth-century critical studies of the Gallican liturgy, defending the early date (no later than the seventh century) and Gothic-Gallican character of the Reichenau libellus against Mone, Theiner, Eichhorn, and J. G. Mueller.

w: Sermon in the Presence of Augustine

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes the author of this text; they treat three unrelated namesakes (Heraclius of Jerusalem, c. 1128–1190/91, Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem; Heraclianus, bishop of Chalcedon against the Manichaeans known only through Photius; and the Byzantine emperor Heraclius, r. 610–641). None fits a Latin sermon printed in Migne's volume of Augustine's works (PL 39), so their biographies are set aside. What can be said comes from the library record alone: a short Latin sermon delivered in Augustine's presence, treating grace, Scripture, and the ministry of preaching.
b.s: The single work held is a brief sermon preached before Augustine, arguing that Christ himself speaks through his ministers, that divine treasure in earthen vessels justifies weak preachers, and that grace patiently labors to overcome hardened hearts while God gives the increase to human cultivation.

b.bio: Eraclus (also printed Eraclius or Evraclus), bishop of Liège from his consecration on 21 August 959 until his death on 27–28 October 971. Educated by Rathier and formerly a dignitary (dean or provost) at Bonn, he was elected with the support of Bruno of Cologne. He founded the collegiate churches of St Paul's (later Liège Cathedral) and St Martin's, promoted scholarship at Liège, accompanied Otto I to Italy in 968, and attributed a personal healing to Martin of Tours. The sources differ on his ordinal among the bishops of Liège; Wikipedia counts him as the twenty-fifth, McClintock and Strong as the sixteenth.
b.s: The two short pieces held here are his letter to Rathier and his account of being healed through Martin of Tours — texts that record how a tenth-century bishop understood saints' healing power, perpetual canonical incorporation by miracle, and commemoration of the dead.

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes this Henricus Floresius: they cover Henrik Florinus (a Finnish priest, 1633–1705), Henricus Sedulius (a Franciscan, 1547–1621), and Henricus Canisius (a canonist, 1562–1610), none of whom fits the library's holdings. The five-page preliminary notice printed under his name in PL 170 concerns the Historia Compostelana: it defends the work's authority against Baronius, Pagi, Pellicer, Ferreras, Vaseo, and Ambrosio de Morales, argues that its three authors wrote it and that it preserves Santiago's pallium and metropolitan status along with unique papal and European records, and insists on the necessity of publishing it.
b.s: He matters here as the editor whose prefatory notice in PL 170 defends the Historia Compostelana as an eyewitness source for the origins of the see of Santiago de Compostela.

b.bio: Born Heinrich Loriti at Mollis in the canton of Glarus, he took the name Glareanus from his birthplace after 1511. He studied philosophy, theology, mathematics and music at the University of Cologne (MA 1510), was crowned poet laureate by Emperor Maximilian I, and from 1514 taught Greek and Latin at Basel, where he formed a lifelong friendship with Erasmus. Though initially sympathetic to Luther's criticisms, he broke with Zwingli and remained faithful to Rome, eventually settling at Freiburg im Breisgau, where he died on 27/28 March 1563. He is best known as a music theorist for the Dodecachordon (Basel, 1547), but also worked as philologist, geographer and mathematician.
b.s: The library holds only his two-page preface in PL 63, evidence of his role as a Humanist editor of patristic texts rather than as a theological author in his own right.

b.bio: The name Henricus Gravius as it appears in Migne's Patrologia Latina attaches only to an index and notice printed with Wolbero's twelfth-century Commentary on the Song of Songs (PL 195); nothing in the library record establishes who this person was. The biographical sources at hand describe other men of the same name: a Dutch Catholic theologian, printer, and director affiliated with the Vatican Library (born 1536, died 1591), a priest and doctor of theology at Leuven whom Gregory XIV set over the Vatican Library and press, and a professor of law at Leuven who died in Rome in 1623. Neither is demonstrably the author of the PL 195 pieces held here.
b.s: The works under this name in this library are a six-page index and a notice accompanying Wolbero's Commentary on the Song of Songs in PL 195; the author himself remains unidentified.

b.bio: Hadoindus succeeded Bertram as bishop of Le Mans around 623 and attended the councils of Clichy (c. 627) and Reims (627–630); at Chalon-sur-Saône in 650 he was represented by Abbot Chagnoaldus. He founded the abbey at Évron and is said to have aided the founding of the monastery of St. Lonegisilus. On February 6, 643 he made a testament naming the church of Le Mans his heir. His cult is attested in the ninth century, when Bishop Aldric translated his relics to the cathedral.
b.s: The work held here concerns episcopal testaments and church property law — testamentary mandates binding executors after death and precarial usufruct leaving ownership with the granting church — matters Hadoindus himself practiced in his own will of 643 leaving the church of Le Mans his heir.

w: Sermon on the feast of St. Vedast

b.bio: Haimin was a monk and teacher (scholasticus) at the abbey of Saint-Vaast in Arras and a pupil of Alcuin. Sources disagree on his death date: Deutsche Biographie gives 834, while Geschichtsquellen gives after 845. He is known chiefly for the Miracula sancti Vedasti, an account of miracles of St. Vedast worked before the mid-ninth century. The works held here under his name are letters and a sermon on the feast of St. Vedast.
b.s: His works here defend the reality of saintly healings and intercession, arguing that miracles signify the spiritual grace they prefigure and that saints continue to aid the faithful after death.

b.bio: Halinard was a Burgundian noble who became a Benedictine monk at Saint-Bénigne in Dijon against his parents' wishes, served as the monastery's provost, and was its abbot from 1031 to 1052. As abbot he wrote to Pope John XIX seeking papal protection for the monastery's cemetery rights against the canons of Dijon cathedral. In 1046 he became Archbishop of Lyon at Pope Gregory VI's command, refusing the emperor's oath of fidelity, and served as counselor to Emperor Henry III and Pope Victor II. The two pages held here are letters concerning the monastery's claims over a granted church.
b.s: The letters here document how an eleventh-century abbot defended monastic property rights by appeal to the pope, prayer over canvassing in choosing a successor, and anathema as legal protection.

b.bio: A Benedictine born in Ponthieu and given as a child oblate to the abbey of Saint-Riquier, Hariulf wrote there at his fellow monks' request the Chronicon Centulense, covering 625–1088 and later extended to 1096. In 1105 he was elected abbot of Saint Peter's in Oudenburg in Flanders, where he served until his death and wrote a biography of Bishop Arnold of Soissons for his canonization. His chronicle preserves information lost when Saint-Riquier's archives burned in 1131; his autograph manuscript was destroyed by fire in 1719 but survives through André Duchesne's copy.
b.s: The library holds his Life of Abbot Angelrannus, which defends Angelrannus's abbatial election against rival claimants — the monks of Saint-Ouen, Hucbert, and Count Angelrannus of Ponthieu and other predators — and presents him as edifying his monks by example and word.

b.bio: Harmotus of Saint Gall (also printed Hartmotus, Haremuthus) was a German Benedictine monk and abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall. Wikisource places him in the ninth century with a floruit extending into the tenth; Alcuin gives his death as 885. The works preserved under his name are epigraphic and commemorative: inscriptions for the temple of Saint Othmar and an epitaph for Grimaldus.
b.s: The library holds his two surviving pieces from PL 126 — the Epitaphium Grimaldi and the Inscriptiones in templo Sancti Othmari — short Latin verse texts treating true worship, wisdom's splendor over sun and gold, and pardon granted to the contrite who pray.

b.bio: Hartmann appears in the monks' register of Saint Gall as deacon by 895, as a document scribe in 897, four times as camerarius between 910 and 912, and as provost in 920. He was elected abbot in 922, succeeding Solomon III after an interregnum of one year; his abbacy is attested in one imprecisely dated document and is listed as lasting three years and four months. Ekkehart IV, the abbey's historian, reports that Hartmann attended to the school and choral singing but neglected administration of the abbey's goods. He is thought to have written a lost account of the history of his times.
b.s: The library holds his poems under PL 116; note that the hymns attributed to an eponymous author are considered unlikely to be his work.

b.bio: Hatto was a Swabian by birth who became a Benedictine monk at Fulda and was elected abbot of Reichenau in 888 and of Ellwangen shortly thereafter, before King Arnulf appointed him archbishop of Mainz in September 891. He presided at the synod of Frankfurt (892) and the imperial assembly at Tribur (895), accompanied Arnulf on his Italian campaigns (894 and 895–96), received the pallium from Pope Formosus at Rome on the second expedition, and after Arnulf's death served as co-guardian (with Adelbero, bishop of Augsburg) for Louis the Child. A mass of legend about dark deeds grew up around his name after his death. The epistle held here defends the Bavarian bishops as slandered innocents, brands their Moravian opponents before the pope, and asserts papal power to absolve by the keys alongside princely coercion of schismatics.
b.s: His letter is a window into Carolingian episcopal politics: defense of bishops against lay accusation, appeals to Rome, and the alliance of secular princes with ecclesiastical discipline.

b.bio: Herbernus (also spelled Hibernus or Erbernus) was first abbot of Marmoutier and afterwards archbishop of Tours; the manuscript titles of his work on Martin record both offices. Sources report that he suffered much from the Norse raids on Touraine and was a devoted cultor of his predecessor Martin. No dates for his life are given in the sources consulted. Some writers styled him a saint, others only venerable; the Bollandist Elenchus lists him as Hibernus.
b.s: The library holds his Miracles of Saint Martin (PL 129), an account of wonders worked after the deposition of Martin's body, arguing that healing comes through the saint's intercession, that relics work miracles for the faithful, and that confession absolves sin and defeats demonic accusation.

w: Epitome of the Life of King Robert
Life of Robert, King of the Franks

b.bio: Helgaud (Helgaldus) was a Benedictine monk of Fleury, raised in the abbey under Abbots Abbo and Gauzlin, where he served as cantor and treasurer before becoming a priest. He undertook a mission to King Robert II the Pious around 1022 and later served as the king's chaplain. His Epitoma vitae regis Rotberti Pii presents Robert as a saintly ruler — curing the blind, submitting to robbery by beggars — against critics who denied the king's salvation. Earlier editors judged the work of little historical value; it is now valued both for what it shows of Robert's reign and private life and as evidence of a stage in medieval history writing. The sole manuscript is Vatican BAV Reg. lat. 566.
b.s: His works here are a hagiographic life of Robert II defending the king's sanctity and salvation, alongside material asserting monastic rights over donated property under the Rule of Benedict.

b.bio: A monk of Saint Gall known from a single work, the Liber de computo. In its preface Helpericus writes humbly to his abbot Aspro, explaining that he had composed the treatise in plain language at the request of junior brothers and sent a copy for examination while on an embassy of Grandval brothers to Auxerre.
b.s: His De computo is a practical textbook of computus, teaching the solar year of 365 days and a quadrant, the bissextile intercalation every fourth year, and the displacement of seasons and solstices when it is neglected, against those who delay the saltus to November or keep Easter with the Jews.

w: On the Growth of the Church of Worcester

b.bio: Hemming was a monk of Worcester Cathedral Priory, later its sub-prior, active in the decades after the Norman Conquest. His Scandinavian name may point to Scandinavian ancestry. He is named in the Worcester Liber Vitae and in a chapter list compiled under Bishop Samson (1096–1112). He compiled the second part of the work now called Hemming's Cartulary, gathering charters with narratives defending the church's property.
b.s: His cartulary and Life of St. Wulstan are the principal witnesses to Worcester's lands and to Bishop Wulfstan, arguing that lands taken by French invaders and powerful men ought to be restored and that written charters secure the church's rights.

w: 8th Life of St. Thomas of Canterbury

b.bio:
Henricus Croilandiae (c. 1200) — The library prints this author as Henricus Croilandiae, and its single holding is an eighth Life of St Thomas of Canterbury preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 190. The only biographical source available here is the Oxford DNB article on a Crowland (Croyland) hagiographer active around 1200, a Benedictine monk who wrote on Becket — but that article names him Roger, not Henry. Whether the printed 'Henricus' is a variant, a scribal attribution, or a distinct person cannot be settled from these sources, so the biographical details are given only as hedged and possibly inapplicable. What can be said rests on the text itself: it compiles from named eyewitness authorities — John of Salisbury, Alan of Tewkesbury, Benedict of Peterborough, Herbert of Bosham, William subprior of Canterbury — and presents Becket's death as martyrdom that vindicated the church's liberty against secular power.

Rogerius Croilandiae (fl. c. 1200) — Roger of Crowland was a Benedictine monk and hagiographer active around 1200. He should not be confused with Roger of Forde, the Cistercian monk of Ford in Devonshire who wrote an account of the revelations of Elizabeth of Schönau, nor with Roger of Wendover, the historian and prior of Belvoir who died in 1236; the work held here belongs to the Crowland author. His surviving claim on attention rests on the eighth life of Thomas Becket printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 190), a compilation that assembles material from earlier eyewitness writers.
b.s: His Life of Becket is a compilation-history that argues the archbishop's martyrdom settled the investiture controversy and defended the universal church against royal control.

b.bio: Henry I, son of Robert II and Constance of Arles, was born at Reims and crowned co-king there in 1027 before succeeding his father in 1031. His reign saw the royal demesne reach its smallest extent under the early Capetians, though some historians judge him a realistic ruler working within the monarchy's limits. He married Matilda of Frisia and then Anne of Kiev; Philip I succeeded him. The works held here are not theological treatises but royal diplomas: charters confirming ecclesiastical endowments, settling church property disputes against castellans, lay holders such as Frotmundus, and Robert of Coucy, and asserting that churches serving the king merit special recompense. They are printed in PL 151 from Mabillon and Martène.
b.s: His diplomas show how an eleventh-century king exercised judgment over church property and framed royal protection of churches as pious duty.

b.bio: Henry of France, third son of King Louis VI of France and Adelaide of Maurienne, was tonsured at thirteen and held several royal abbeys before Bernard of Clairvaux converted him in 1146 to the Cistercian life at Clairvaux. Elected bishop of Beauvais in 1149 on the death of Bishop Odo III, he clashed with the burghers and with King Louis VII. In 1161 he became archbishop of Reims, where his correspondence shows him administering the metropolitan court — one letter here asserts that an appeal to a higher judge suspends the jurisdiction of the lower — and affirming obedience to Pope Alexander III against the antipope Victor (Octavian) and his partisans.
b.s: The letters and diplomas here are chiefly administrative and polemical: instruments of metropolitan jurisdiction and of loyalty to Pope Alexander III during the 1159 schism, not doctrinal treatises.

b.bio: The library holds one two-page sermon on the Lord's Passover under the name Henry of Parma, printed in PL 139. None of the consulted sources describes an author of this name: they cover John of Parma (Franciscan minister general, 1208–1289), Henry of Kalkar (Carthusian, 1328–1408), and Henry of Friemar the Elder (Augustinian, c. 1245–1340), none of whom is credited with this work. The attribution of the sermon to a 'Henry of Parma' therefore rests on the Migne volume alone, and no dates or biographical facts for such a person are established by these sources.
b.s: The sermon here is an allegorical exegesis of the Passover: pascha as passage from darkness to light, the wounded traveler as fallen humanity, Christ as the true healer, with details such as the loins girt and shoes of dead skins read morally.

b.bio: The library's single work under this name is an eight-page letter addressed to a Stephen, written in defense of Jerome, abbot of Pomposa, against envious and superstitious critics. The author cites Augustine most often, alongside Jerome of Pomposa himself, Gregory, Isidore of Seville, John Chrysostom, Methodius of Patara, Apponius, and one Guido — the last possibly the celebrated abbot Guido of Pomposa (d. 1046), though neither the letter nor any surviving records confirms this identification. None of The surviving records describes a Henry of Pomposa; they cover Henry of Settimello, Henry of Avranches, Henry of Valenciennes, and St. Guido of Pomposa, all different persons, so nothing can be asserted here about the author's life or dates.
b.s: His letter is a small witness to the literary culture of Pomposa Abbey, defending the reading of pagan books in Christian libraries and arguing that scriptural knowledge is needed to discern virtue.

w: Treatise on the Purgatory of St. Patrick

b.bio: Henry of Saltrey (Sawtry) was a Cistercian monk at Saltrey in Huntingdonshire, fl. 1150. From Gilbert of Louth he learned the story of the knight Owen's alleged descent into St Patrick's Purgatory (the cave on an island in Lough Derg), which he committed to writing as the 'Purgatorium Sancti Patricii', addressed to Henry, abbot of Wardon ('Abbas de Sartis'). Seymour infers from dates connected with Gilbert that the account was actually written down c. 1186. The narrative was embodied by Matthew Paris in his Chronica Majora, translated into French verse (including Marie de France's Espurgatoire de Seint Patriz, early 13th century) and into English verse as 'Owayne Miles'.
b.s: His Tractatus de Purgatorio Sancti Patricii is the earliest known account of the knight Owen's vision and did much to spread belief in Lough Derg as purgatory's entrance across medieval Europe.

w: History of the Calamities of the Church of Salzburg

b.bio: None of The surviving records concerns this author: they describe Henry of Friemar (Augustinian, d. 1340), Henry of Avranches (poet, d. 1260), Henry of Kalkar (Carthusian, d. 1408), and Henry of Segusio (canonist, d. 1271) — different men, to be ignored here. The library holds one work under this name, a short history of the calamities of the church of Salzburg, printed in PL 196. Its content places it in an eleventh-century investiture-conflict context: it defends Salzburg against a hostile emperor and Frederick, denounces concubinary clerics and a schismatic episcopate loyal to the emperor, and asserts that communion with the Roman pontiff overrides imperial oath.
b.s: The work is a partisan history from the investiture conflict, arguing that God turns persecutors' malice to the good of the elect and that the church of Salzburg remained free of schism through fidelity to the pope.

w: On the Diversity of Fortune and the Consolation of Philosophy

b.bio: Henry of Settimello (Henricus Septimellensis, 'Henricus Pauper') was an Italian Latin poet of the later twelfth century, born of humble parents at Settimello near Prato. He studied at Bologna, became a priest, and held the benefice of Calenzano in Florentine territory. According to Filippo Villani, a lawsuit brought by the Bishop of Florence stripped him of the benefice and reduced him to poverty; in that condition he composed his elegiac poem on fortune. He is counted Italy's leading Latin poet of the twelfth-century Renaissance.
b.s: His De diversitate fortunae et philosophiae consolatione is a Boethian consolation in verse arguing that fortune is unstable and treacherous by nature (like Proteus), that true nobility lies in probity rather than lineage, and that death can be salvation for the sufferer.

b.bio: the surviving records describe Gregory of Tours, the sixth-century bishop and historian of the Franks; they do not describe this author and cannot be used here. The library's record points elsewhere: the works held appear in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 121, which collects ninth-century material, and their content — synodal chapters on ordination, penance for diviners, usury, and clerical conduct, a commonitorium, and a piece on the Annunciation citing Leo and 'Charles the glorious king' — fits a Carolingian churchman named Herard of Tours rather than the Merovingian historian. Nothing in surviving records or the library record gives dates or offices for him.
b.s: The works held here are Carolingian disciplinary texts: synodal chapters regulating clergy, worship, sacraments, baptism, prayer, and penance — including public penance for sorcerers and diviners, prohibition of usury, gradual ordination with examination of candidates, clerics barred from secular business, and clerical disputes judged by the bishop — valuable as evidence of Frankish church order rather than as history.

b.bio: The library prints the name as Herbert of Torres. Sources identify him as a French Cistercian, third abbot of Mores from 1165 or 1168, who resigned in 1178 and retired to Clairvaux as chaplain and secretary to Henry of Marcy. There he probably met Gonario de Lacon, former judge of Torres, whose see he became archbishop of in 1181. He withdrew to the monastery of Cabuabbas, where he died; one source gives his death as between 4 July and 11 August 1198, another as 28 February 1196 at Turris (Porto Torres). A different Herbert of Bosham, Becket's biographer, is not this man.
b.s: His Liber miraculorum et visionum, recording what he saw at Mores, Clairvaux and Torres, circulated widely in the Middle Ages (22 manuscripts survive) and was edited by Chifflet in 1660 and reprinted by Migne in PL 198.

b.bio: Heriger studied at the cathedral school of Liège, then became a Benedictine monk at Lobbes, where he served for many years as scholasticus of the monastic school. In 990 he was elected to succeed Folcwin as Abbot of Lobbes, an office he held until his death on 31 October 1007. He was an intimate friend of Bishop Notger of Liège, whom he accompanied to Rome in 989 and at whose instance he wrote several historical works. His pupils included Burchard of Worms, Adalbold of Utrecht, Olbert of Gembloux, Wazo of Liège, and Hugo, later abbot of Lobbes.
b.s: The sources describe him as writing with more historical criticism than most of his contemporaries, though as a hagiographer he sometimes sinks to the level of an ascetical novelist. His chief work is the Gesta episcoporum Leodiensium, which reaches only to the death of St. Remaclus in 667. Note: the library record for this volume also shows strongly doctrinal and exegetical material (on creation ex nihilo, the eternal Word begotten from God's essence, polemic against the pseudo-Clementine decretals and Arians), so the held works are not purely historical and hagiographical.

w: Deeds of the Bishops of Liège
Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège

b.bio:
Hereger of Lobbes (c. 925 – 31 October 1007) — Heriger studied at the cathedral school of Liège, then became a Benedictine monk at Lobbes, where he served for many years as scholasticus of the monastic school. In 990 he was elected to succeed Folcwin as Abbot of Lobbes, an office he held until his death on 31 October 1007. He was an intimate friend of Bishop Notger of Liège, whom he accompanied to Rome in 989 and at whose instance he wrote several historical works. His pupils included Burchard of Worms, Adalbold of Utrecht, Olbert of Gembloux, Wazo of Liège, and Hugo, later abbot of Lobbes.

Anselm of Liège (c. 1008–1056) — Anselm of Liège was educated at the episcopal school of Liège and became canon and later dean of the cathedral. Sources disagree on his origins: most give his birth as 1008; Encyclopedia.com says he was born near Cologne probably in the late tenth century and died after March 3, 1056. He was esteemed by Bishop Wazo of Liège and by Bishop Theoduin, whom he accompanied to Rome in 1053–54. At the request of his godmother (or aunt) Ida, Abbess of St. Cecilia in Cologne, he wrote his Gesta Episcoporum Tungrensium, Trajectensium et Leodiensium, continuing Heriger of Lobbes's chronicle of the first twenty-seven bishops and adding twenty-five more down to Wazo.
b.s: The sources describe him as writing with more historical criticism than most of his contemporaries, though as a hagiographer he sometimes sinks to the level of an ascetical novelist. His chief work is the Gesta episcoporum Leodiensium, which reaches only to the death of St. Remaclus in 667. Note: the library record for this volume also shows strongly doctrinal and exegetical material (on creation ex nihilo, the eternal Word begotten from God's essence, polemic against the pseudo-Clementine decretals and Arians), so the held works are not purely historical and hagiographical.

b.bio: Heribert was bishop of Eichstätt from 1022 until his death on 24 July 1042 in or near Freising. He came from the high-noble Rhenish-Franconian family of the Konradiner, with property chiefly in the Wormsgau, and was a nephew of Bishop Heinrich I of Würzburg and of Archbishop Heribert of Cologne; he was also related to Abbot Williram of Ebersberg. Together with his brother Gez(e)mann he attended the Würzburg cathedral school, where he became a canon. He was installed by Emperor Henry II, apparently as a counterweight to noble/ducal power-building in Bavaria and Swabia, and accompanied the king on several journeys through the Reich. He was a gifted hymn writer whose hymns survive in numerous manuscripts.
b.s: The library holds his hymns (PL 141), which treat the adoration of the cross, cleansing from original and actual sin through Christ's holy cross by divine pity, coequal worship owed to the three persons, baptism (the baptized remain assailed by sin after cleansing), the intercession of saints and angelic orders for the faithful's salvation, God as fountain of all goods, and last things/eternal life.

b.bio: A monk named Heribert who wrote against the heretics of Périgord, apparently in the twelfth century. His work survives in PL 181. No source in the provided set concerns this author (they all treat St. Heribert of Cologne, a different man), so nothing further can be stated about his dates or monastery.
b.s: His single held work, On the Heretics of Périgord, is a Latin account and refutation of a southern French dissenting movement, treating the Church, the Lord's Supper, and true worship while warning against false prophets.

w: On the Translation of St. Clement

b.bio: Herimann of Metz as printed here is Herman of Tournai (also called Herman of Laon; Latin Herimannus), third abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai. A pupil of Odoardus, later bishop of Cambrai, he was expelled from his abbacy in 1136 by a faction claiming lax enforcement of the Benedictine rule, and while at Rome wrote the Restauratio sancti Martini Tornacensis, an account of his abbey's refounding and fortunes. The two pieces held here — a charter restoring market revenue taken from the monastery by faction, and an account of the translation of St. Clement's relics — belong to that abbey-centered corpus.
b.s: His writings preserve a monk's-eye social history of eleventh- and twelfth-century Lotharingia, and the works here document a monastery's economic rights and its cult of relics.

w: On the Measurement of the Astrolabe
On the Uses of the Astrolabe
Poem on the Conflict between the Sheep and the Flax
Sequence for the Blessed Virgin Mary

b.bio: Hermann of Reichenau (Hermannus Contractus), son of Count Wolverad II von Altshausen, was born in Swabia in 1013 and disabled from birth. Entrusted at about age seven to Abbot Berno of Reichenau, he took monastic vows there in 1043 and spent his life on the island. He wrote on history, mathematics, astronomy, music theory, and hymnody; the sources note his role in transmitting Arabic learning and instruments into central Europe. The library holds his world chronicle, treatises on the astrolabe, musical works, a Marian sequence, and an allegorical poem on the conflict between the sheep and the flax. Sources differ on his birthplace (Altshausen or Saulgau), his birthday (18 July or 18 February), and death day (21 or 24 September).
b.s: His chronicle here is a citation-heavy universal history from creation to his own century, drawing on Fulda and Metz annals, Bede, Paul the Deacon, and others, while his astrolabe and music treatises show the same eleventh-century monastery joining history, polemic against Arians and Ptolemy, and technical science.

b.bio: Heriveus (Latin Hervaeus), archbishop of Reims from his ordination on 6 July 900 until his death on 2 July 922, was a West Frankish churchman who had served as a notary in the royal chancery under King Odo and then Charles the Simple before succeeding the murdered Fulk at Reims. Flodoard of Reims, who knew him, records his administration of the see: translations of relics including St Remigius, rebuilding of fortifications damaged by Viking raids, and an agreement with Archbishop Hatto of Mainz in 902. The Cyclopedia adds that he became chancellor of France in 910.
b.s: The library holds a single letter to Wito, a penitential treatise defending tearful repentance and enjoined penance for grave sinners against Novatians, Donatists, and rebaptizing heretics, and against bishops of Gaul who denied deathbed penance.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies a 'Hervard of Liège.' The surviving records describe two other Liège figures: Alger of Liège (c. 1055–1131), a canonist who served at St. Bartholomew's and St. Lambert's Cathedral in Liège, acted as secretary to Bishop Otbert, and retired to Cluny after 1121 (source:1, source:4); and Heriger of Lobbes (c. 925–1007), Benedictine monk, scholasticus and abbot of Lobbes (990–1007), author of the Gesta episcoporum Leodiensium (source:2, source:3). Neither is this author, and neither can be conflated with him. The library holds under the name 'Hervard of Liège' a single short letter in PL 211 concerning Guibert, urging resignation of office to avoid scandal, defending the suffrages and veneration of saints, and teaching that God hears only the prayers of the charitable.
b.s: The work held here is a brief exhortatory letter on humility in office, prayer, and the veneration of saints, citing Guibert Martin.

w: On the Peace Treaty between Callistus II and Henry V
Short Commentary on the Peace Treaty between Calixtus II and Henry V

b.bio: Hesso was a cathedral canon and scholasticus at Strasbourg, attested in documents for the years 1116–1119. He wrote an account of the Council of Reims and a brief description of how the dispute between King Henry V and Pope Calixtus II over investitures began and moved toward settlement. The library's two short works under his name are both accounts of the peace negotiated between Calixtus II and Henry V. Catalogues list variant forms of his name connecting him to Reims as well as Strasbourg.
b.s: His works here are contemporary accounts of the Concordat struggle between Calixtus II and Henry V, arguing that renouncing lay investiture costs the king nothing in temporal rights while ending the simoniacal heresy.

w: On the Vision and Death of Wetti

b.bio: Hetto of Basel (Haito, Hatto, Heito) was a Swabian noble who entered Reichenau Abbey at age five and later headed its monastic school. He became bishop of Basel in 802 (some authorities say 805) and abbot of Reichenau in 806, holding both until illness forced his resignation in 823, after which he lived as a simple monk at Reichenau. Charlemagne trusted him: he went on the 811 embassy to Constantinople. He rebuilt the Basel cathedral and issued capitularies regulating clergy conduct, revealing both clerical ignorance and reforming effort.
b.s: The works held here — the Vision of Wetti and two capitularies — show a Carolingian reformer legislating priestly discipline, liturgy, marriage law, and moral teaching for clergy and people.

b.bio: A Benedictine monk of Hirsau in Swabia, attested there between 1088 and about 1100; sources style him Haimo Prior Hirsaugiensis. He wrote the Vita Willihelmi abbatis Hirsaugiensis, a life of Abbot William of Hirsau, datable to before about 1107. He must not be confused with Haymo of Halberstadt, the ninth-century Benedictine bishop who died on 26 March 853, nor with the anonymous monk 'Emmo' to whom some scholars assign other works printed under this name.
b.s: His Life of William is a narrative source for Abbot William of Hirsau and the Hirsau reform; the text as preserved argues that monasteries ought to be freed from lay lordship by imperial and papal privilege and records how monastic customs were adapted from Cluny to local conditions.

w: Prologue to the Chronicle of Liutprand

b.bio: Jerónimo Román de la Higuera was born in Toledo on 28 August 1538 and died there in 1611 (sources give the day as 14 November or 14 September). He studied arts and theology at Toledo, entered the Jesuit order at Alcalá de Henares as a novice in December 1562, professed final vows in 1590 at Ocaña, and taught Latin grammar and humanities in Jesuit colleges while serving as a priest. He printed nothing in his lifetime but circulated manuscripts, including the forged 'false chronicles' attributed to Flavius Lucius Dexter, Maximus, and others, published posthumously by Bivar at Saragossa in 1619.
b.s: The work held here is his prologue to a chronicle under the name of Liutprand, part of the corpus of fabricated early Spanish chronicles that misled scholarship for two centuries before being exposed as Higuera's inventions.

b.bio: Hilarius, printed here as 'discipulus Abaelardi', was a Latin elegiac poet who studied under Peter Abelard and addressed verses to him, including one with a French refrain ('Tort avers vos li mestre') when Abelard threatened to stop teaching. He may later have made his way to Angers; after about 1125 no certain trace of him remains. Sources disagree on his identity: some identify him with Hilary of Orléans, teacher of classical texts mentioned by William of Tyre around 1150 (the IdRef authority record merges these figures and adds unverified details such as dates 1075?–1140?, a canonry at Le Ronceray, and professorships at Orléans and Angers); others treat these as separate men. His poems survive in Paris, BnF supp. lat. 1008, edited by Champollion-Figeac in 1838 as Hilarii versus et ludi.
b.s: The library holds from him only a single-page Elegy in PL 178, but he matters as one of Abelard's pupils whose light verse and religious plays preserve the voice of the Paraclete circle.

b.bio: Hildemar was a Carolingian monk, associated with Corbie and later abbot of Civitate in Lombardy. He is known chiefly for the Expositio Regulae Sancti Benedicti, a long commentary on the Rule of St Benedict transmitted under his name (also circulating as the Ps.-Paulus Diaconus Commentarium and a Ps.-Basilius version). The library holds from him only a short letter to Ursus of Benevento on reading aloud in church: it treats punctuation as the basis of distinct delivery, maps grave, acute, and circumflex accents onto high, middle, and low punctuations, assigns acute to short vowels and circumflex to long ones, and discusses interrogative inflection, citing Donatus, Isidore, Sergius, Pompeius, and Augustine.
b.s: His letter is a Carolingian witness to how punctuation and accent theory governed liturgical reading; his commentary on the Benedictine Rule was widely transmitted in several recensions.

b.bio: Heiric of Auxerre (the library prints his name as 'Hilderic', apparently in error) was a French Benedictine theologian of Saint-Germain d'Auxerre, born in 841 and an oblate there from about age seven. He studied under Haimo of Auxerre, with Lupus Servatus at Ferrières (859–860), and at Saint-Médard de Soissons (862–865), where he came into contact with John Scotus Eriugena. He then returned to Auxerre and taught there until his death in 876; his students included Remigius of Auxerre and Hucbald.
b.s: The two poems held here — a metrical letter and an epitaph — carry doctrinal verse: creation from nothing, divine simplicity and eternity, the Trinity, redemption through Christ's blood applied by spirit and water, and the efficacy of the saints' prayers for the faithful dead. His chief work elsewhere was a metrical Life of St. Germanus of Auxerre dedicated to Charles the Bald around 876.

b.bio: Honoratus, bishop of Marseille in the latter fifth century, was a spiritual student of Honoratus of Arles and a preacher whom Gennadius describes as of ready and abundant eloquence. He wrote homilies against heresy and lives of church leaders; his correspondence with Pope Gelasius I on orthodoxy is lost. The Life of Hilary of Arles held here is generally attributed to him, though an Arles manuscript assigns it to Reverentius (Ravennius), Hilary's successor.
b.s: His Life of Hilary of Arles is among the few surviving Gallic saints' lives of the period, presenting humility, mortification, and contempt for worldly goods as the substance of sanctity.

b.bio: Lamberto Scannabecchi, born at Fagnano near Imola of humble parents (sources give his birth as 9 February 1060 or an unknown date), was archdeacon of Bologna before Paschal II called him to Rome. He became cardinal-priest of Santa Prassede and in 1117 cardinal-bishop of Ostia and Velletri. As Calixtus II's legate to Henry V he was chiefly instrumental in negotiating the Concordat of Worms (1122), ending the investiture controversy. Elected pope in late December 1124 after a contested vote against Celestine II, he preserved the Worms settlement, favored new orders such as the Cistercians and Augustinians, approved the Knights Templar in 1128, and died in Rome on 13/14 February 1130.
b.s: The works held here are his letters and privileges: instruments asserting papal protection of monastic houses, free burial except for excommunicates, obedience owed to prelates, and excommunication for violation of papal privilege — the documentary machinery by which the post-Worms papacy extended its jurisdiction.

b.bio: Howel Dha (Hywel ap Cadell), who became sole king of Seisyllwg in 920 and shortly thereafter established Deheubarth, eventually ruling most of Wales, is recorded as King of the Britons in the Annales Cambriae and Annals of Ulster. The Leges Ecclesiasticae printed under his name (PL 138) opens with his own words: seeing the Welsh abuse their laws, he summoned six laymen and all the clergy of each cantref to Ty Gwyn above the Taff, kept Lent there in fasting and prayer, and with twelve learned laymen and one cleric, Blangoridus, drew up the laws in three parts — the law of the daily court, the law of the country, and the usages of both. The dates given here are those assigned to the text in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 138; Hywel's birth and death years are not fixed by these sources.
b.s: The work held here is the ecclesiastical portion of the Laws of Hywel Dda, the foundational codification of Welsh law, treating clerical immunity from homicide-price and vengeance, synodal judgment of injuries to priests, judicial oaths against false judgment for bribe or favor, and the claim that only the church shelters violators of the king's peace.

w: History of the Ascension of the Lord
History of the Conversion of Proterius
History of the Passion of St. Agnes
History of the Passion of the Illustrious St. Dionysius

The Fall and Conversion of Theophilus the Vicedominus

b.bio: A Saxon secular canoness of Gandersheim Abbey, born to Saxon nobles around 930–940 and educated there under Rikkardis and Gerberga, niece of Otto I and later abbess (959–1001). Sources differ on her death date: the Springer encyclopedia gives c. 1000, the Catholic Encyclopedia about 1002, and Wikipedia c. 973. She wrote Latin drama, saints' lives, and historical poems under Ottonian patronage; she is depicted presenting her Gesta Oddonis to Otto the Great.
b.s: The first dramatist of the Latin West after antiquity and the first known female writer of the Germanosphere; her six comedies answer Terence with Christian heroines whose virginity and martyrdom triumph over pagan persecutors.

b.bio: Hugo Edessensi is the Latin archbishop of Edessa, a Fleming who joined the Cluniac confraternity on his way to Jerusalem and held the see from about 1120 until his death. He defended Edessa during Zengi's siege of 1144 and was killed when the city fell. The letter printed under his name in PL 155 addresses the archbishop of Reims and confirms the authenticity of relics by ecclesiastical testimony and seal, citing Gerard the archdeacon, Stephen the dean, and Theso the treasurer as witnesses.
b.s: His single surviving letter documents how relic authentication was conducted through named clerical witnesses and seals in the twelfth-century Latin East.

w: On the Miracles of the Blessed Virgin Mary

b.bio: Hugh Farsit (Hugo Farsitus), also called Hugh of Soissons, was a canon regular of Saint-Jean-des-Vignes born late in the 11th century. Between about 1111 and 1115 he wrote the Otium for his sister Helvide, a four-book collection of theological and moral reflections with autobiographical elements; he mentions four earlier works now lost. Sometime after 1132, probably after the death of Abbess Mathilde I de la Ferté-sous-Jouarre in December 1143, he began work on his Little Book of Miracles of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the City of Soissons, probably at the request of the nuns of Notre-Dame de Soissons and Abbess Mathilde II. The library prints him as Hugh Farsitus.
b.s: His one work held here is a miracle collection recording wonders worked through the Virgin Mary at Soissons between 1128 and 1132 during the abbacy of Mathilde I — an early witness to Marian devotion, intercession, relics, and healing in twelfth-century France.

b.bio: Born about 1064, probably at Verdun, into a prominent family; educated and professed at St-Vannes, Verdun. When Bishop Dietrich backed Henry IV and antipope Clement III, the pro-papal abbot left with his monks to St-Bénigne at Dijon, where Hugh made vows under Abbot Jarento, a friend of Gregory VII, and accompanied him on a 1096 mission to Normandy and England. Elected Abbot of Flavigny in 1096, he quarrelled with the Bishop of Autun and his own monks, fled twice, and abdicated despite the Council of Valence (1100) ordering his reinstatement. The library's record also preserves a tradition that Richard of Verdun installed him as abbot in 1111 for a three-year term.
b.s: His Chronicle preserves historical material found nowhere else, though Lambert, Berthold, and Bernold surpass him as historians; the works here are chiefly historical rather than doctrinal.

w: Excerpts from the cartulary of the Church of Grenoble

b.bio: Hugh of Châteauneuf, called Hugh of Grenoble, was born at Châteauneuf-sur-Isère (Châteauneuf-d'Isère, Dauphiné) around 1052–1053 and became a canon of Valence while still a layman. Elected bishop of Grenoble in 1080 while still unordained, he was consecrated by Pope Gregory VII and held the see for over fifty years. A partisan of the Gregorian reform, he opposed the Archbishop of Vienne, the later Pope Callixtus II, and welcomed Bruno of Cologne's Carthusians to La Grande Chartreuse in 1084. He was canonized by Innocent II in 1134.
b.s: The works here are his cartulary excerpts and letters defending Grenoble's church property against Guido, Archbishop of Vienne, arguing that long peaceful possession proves rightful ownership, that royal grants founded Grenoble's title, that bare rumor cannot defeat documented possession, and that privilege obtained by subreption is void; they also argue that a pope with a council may restore rightful investiture and release churches from disobedient metropolitans.

b.bio: Hugh was son of Count Theobald III of Blois and Adelaide of Vermandois (called Adele of Valois in some accounts); on his brother Odo's death in 1093 he took Troyes, Vitry and Bar-sur-Aube, the core of what became the county of Champagne. He led crusading ventures in 1104–1107 and 1114–1116, gave the valley on which Clairvaux Abbey was built, and in 1125 left his lands to his nephew Theobald to join the Templars in Jerusalem. The single item held here, however, is a one-page epistle concerning synodal arbitration between monasteries (Saint-Aubin of Angers, La Trinité de Vendôme) citing bishops of Nevers and Meaux; whether the count or another Hugh of Troyes wrote it cannot be settled from the sources given.
b.s: The work held here records how synodal authority adjudicated disputes between monasteries in early twelfth-century France; its attribution to the famous count is uncertain.

b.bio: The library prints this name as Hugh II of Nevers. the surviving records describe other bearers of the name: Bishop Hugh III of Nevers, a Burgundian bishop from a vicecomital family whose first year in office was 1074, and an otherwise unattested Hugh of Nevers, brother of Count William II, named only in a charter of 1144. Neither source gives dates or career details for a Hugh II, so none are asserted here. The single work held under this name is a one-page epistle to Bartholomew of Tours concerning a church dispute.
b.s: His letter here is evidence for property disputes between monasteries and episcopal authority in medieval France, arguing that a fief cannot be alienated without the lord's consent and that the church of Credon belongs to Holy Trinity abbey of Vendôme, against the monks of Saint-Aubin.

b.bio: Born at Avalon in Burgundy — sources give the birth year variously as about 1135 or about 1140 — Hugh entered the canons regular at Villard-Benoît with his father, then joined La Grande Chartreuse around 1165. He became bishop of Lincoln and died in London on 16 November 1200. He was canonized in 1220. The works held here are not treatises but episcopal acta: diplomas confirming monastic possessions and grants in alms, and letters of visitation defending such grants against simoniacal encroachment.
b.s: The library holds his administrative charters and visitation letters, which show a twelfth-century bishop exercising canonical authority to protect donations given to religious houses and the poor.

w: On the Body and Blood of Christ against Berengar

b.bio: Hugh of Langres was bishop of Langres, son of Gilduin, Count of Breteuil, and wrote in Latin. He met Berengar of Tours and discussed his views with him at length before writing De corpore et sanguine Christi against him. At the Council of Rheims in 1049 he faced a range of accusations; Halinard of Lyon conceded he was guilty of simony and extortion but not the other charges. Hugh fled the council, was deposed and excommunicated, went to Rome in 1050 to confess, and died on the journey back to France.
b.s: His anti-Berengarian treatise is an early eleventh-century defense of a real change in the eucharistic elements: the eucharist is a true body not incorporeal, the bread must cease in nature to be Christ's body (for persistence of the bread's essence would entail no consecratory change), the change is received by faith in divine omnipotence as the incarnation is, and God's word and will exceed all nature.

b.bio: The library's Hugh of Lyon is Hugh of Die (printed here under his later see), born at Romans-sur-Isère around 1040. Prior of Saint-Marcel in Chalon-sur-Saône, he became bishop of Die on 19 October 1073 and was consecrated in Rome by Gregory VII on 9 March 1074. From 1081 he held the metropolitan see of Lyon and served as a papal legate. He convened a synod at Autun (1077) that suspended simoniacal bishops, notably Manasses of Reims, and later presided over an Autun synod whose measures led him to excommunicate Philip I of France over his marriage to Bertrade de Montfort. He was himself excommunicated on 29 August 1087 at Benevento for opposing Victor III's election, then reinstated as legate by Urban II in 1094. He died at Susa on 7 October 1106. Do not confuse him with Hugh of Flavigny (b. c. 1064), a monk-historian who was friendly with him, or with the ninth-century deacon Florus of Lyon.
b.s: His letters and privileges here are Gregorian-reform polemics: suspension of simoniacal and irregularly ordained bishops pending papal judgment, canonical examination before election, perseverance for final salvation, and the intercession of departed saints — argued against Ivo of Chartres, the abbot of Cluny, Daimbert of Sens, and the king of the Franks.

b.bio: Hugh of Mâcon, of the illustrious house of the counts of Mâcon and a childhood friend of Bernard of Clairvaux, entered Cîteaux where he received the monastic habit from Abbot Stephen. He was sent at the head of twelve monks to found Pontigny and became its first abbot. In 1137 he became bishop of Auxerre, described as the first Cistercian raised to the episcopate, and served until his death at Pontigny on 10 October 1151.
b.s: The works held here are a charter and letters to Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis, in which Hugh asserts that hereditary right passes lawfully to wife and children — documents of his activity as bishop and mediator rather than theological treatises.

b.bio: Hugh Metellus (Hugo Metel) was born at Toul in Lorraine and educated at the schools of Chartres and Laon under Anselm of Laon. He entered the abbey of canons regular of Saint-Léon in Toul, probably in the 1120s, and was still writing in the 1140s. Sources give differing death dates: c. 1150 or near 1157. He left fifty-five Latin letters plus poems, addressed to figures including Bernard of Clairvaux, Peter Abelard, and Heloise. The two pages held here are letters defending the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist against a correspondent named Gerland.
b.s: The letters here are twelfth-century eucharistic polemic asserting that the consecrated host is no longer bread but Christ's body, venerable by faith rather than argued by reason, with Augustine cited as teaching the real presence.

w: History of the Monastery of Vézelay

b.bio: Hugh of Poitiers was a Benedictine monk of Vézelay Abbey who died in 1167. He wrote the Historia Vizeliacensis monasterii between about 1140 and 1160 for Abbot Ponce of Vézelay, brother of Peter the Venerable of Cluny. He also wrote a short history of the counts of Nevers. The work is a partisan account of the abbey's affairs and an important source for the history of twelfth-century France.
b.s: The History of the Monastery of Vézelay held here defends the abbey's liberties against the counts of Nevers and the bishop of Autun, recording monastic claims to exemption from exactions, founders' usufruct and advocacy rights, and the monks' intercessory obligations to founders and rulers.

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes this Hugh; they treat Hugh Farsit of Soissons, Hugh of Saint Victor, and Hugh of Saint-Cher, who must be set aside as namesakes. What can be said comes from the works held here: an epistle and a privilege in which he appears as archbishop of Sens, corresponding with Heloise, abbess of the Paraclete, and with the counts Henry, Theobald, and Stephen and the Countess of Blois.
b.s: The two pieces here concern the abbey of the Paraclete: the canonical election of its abbess from the mother church, the entrusting of the souls of the faithful dead to Christ, and the claim that its conventions were irrevocable even against papal intervention.

b.bio: Hugo de Campo Florido was bishop of Soissons; the sources date his activity to 1159–1175 and print his Epistolae in PL 196 (cols. 1585–1588D). The two pages held here are historical letters from the conflict with the Norman party around the bishop of Évreux: one asserts that pilgrims carrying nothing for sale owe no tolls, the other that the bishop remained faithful to the king unto death. Both appeal to the lord pope.
b.s: His surviving letters are brief documentary evidence of episcopal loyalty to the crown and papal arbitration in the Norman disputes of the mid-twelfth century.

w: Commentary on the majorat and seneschalcy of France

b.bio: Hugh of Cleeris was a knight of Anjou, known only from a single work dated 1130: a commentary on the majorate and seneschalcy of France. The commentary argues that the seneschalcy of France was conferred on the counts of Anjou, that the seneschal owes homage to the count of Anjou, and that the count holds judicial supremacy in France, marshalling eyewitness testimony and citations of named figures (Fulk, count of Jerusalem; King Robert; William and Stephen of Garlande; Ralph, count of Péronne; Walter of Senlis) against King Louis.
b.s: His single surviving work is an Angevin legal-historical proof text asserting the counts of Anjou's hereditary claim to the seneschalcy and judicial primacy of France.

b.bio: Hugo de Ribodimonte (Hugo Ribomontensis) is a twelfth-century Latin author, associated in the Bibale database with Saint-Bertin. The sources give no birth or death dates beyond a twelfth-century range; Documenta Catholica Omnia dates his one work to 1125. He wrote an epistle addressed to G., an Angevin (Ad G Andegavensem), preserved in PL 166, cols. 833–836C.
b.s: His single surviving letter answers questions on the soul's origin: it argues that the soul is neither made of corporeal matter nor part of the divine substance nor a body, that it is infused after the body is formed rather than propagated from Adam (against traducians), and that Christ's sinless soul was not derived from Adam's sinful propagation — leaning heavily on Augustine.

w: Observations on the Books of Sentences of Robert Pullen

b.bio: Hugo Mathoud (Hugues Mathoud), born 1622, died 1705, was a Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint-Maur. The library holds four pieces under his name in PL 186 and PL 211: an 'Observations on the Books of Sentences of Robert Pullen' and its accompanying Preface, Scholiast to the reader, and Dedication Letter. These are editorial apparatus for the Sentences of Robert Pullen, the twelfth-century master whom Mathoud's notes argue preceded Peter Lombard in scholastic theology and followed Augustine's doctrine throughout. He also wrote the De vera Senonum origine christiana (Paris: Langronne, 1687), defending the Christian origins of Sens against the critical observations of Jean de Launoy.
b.s: Mathoud matters here as the seventeenth-century Maurist editor whose annotations frame Robert Pullen's Sentences, arguing that Pullus anticipated the Lombard and stood wholly within Augustine's doctrine.

b.bio: Heinrich Meibom (Meibomius), born at Lemgo and died at Helmstedt, was a German historian and Neo-Latin poet of evangelical confession. He wrote on German history as well as Latin verse. He should not be confused with his grandson Johann Heinrich Meibom (1638–1700), the Helmstedt physician who described the meibomian glands, nor with Marcus Meibomius (c. 1630–1710/11), the Danish historian of ancient Greek music.
b.s: The library holds under this name only a single-page historical notice printed in PL 137; readers should treat it as a scholarly notice rather than a patristic text, since Meibom was an early modern German antiquary, not a Latin Father.

b.bio: Hosius was bishop of Corduba in Hispania from about 295 and a confessor during the persecution under Maximian (or Diocletian). He attended the Synod of Elvira around 300/301, then served as Constantine's chief ecclesiastical adviser on the Donatist question and as imperial emissary to the East against Arius (324). Sources credit him with presiding at Nicaea (probably) and at the Council of Serdica; he died between about 357 and 359, either at Sirmium or in Spain.
b.s: The two pieces held here are conciliar texts tied to Serdica: disciplinary canons on episcopal translation, provincial jurisdiction, and appeals to the Roman see, and a letter rebuking Constantius over Arian interference.

b.bio:
Hosius of Corduba (c. c. 256–359) — Hosius was bishop of Corduba in Hispania from about 295 and a confessor during the persecution under Maximian (or Diocletian). He attended the Synod of Elvira around 300/301, then served as Constantine's chief ecclesiastical adviser on the Donatist question and as imperial emissary to the East against Arius (324). Sources credit him with presiding at Nicaea (probably) and at the Council of Serdica; he died between about 357 and 359, either at Sirmium or in Spain.

Council of Sardica (343) — The Council of Sardica met, most probably in 343, at Sardica in Dacia (now Sofia, Bulgaria). It was convoked by the emperors Constans and Constantius at the urging of Pope Julius I, chiefly to settle the case of Athanasius and other bishops condemned and vindicated by rival Eastern and Western councils. Hosius of Corduba presided over the sessions of the Western majority after the Eastern bishops withdrew. The council's doctrinal sessions failed to reunite the parties, but its disciplinary canons proved influential: they regulated episcopal translation, provincial jurisdiction, and — most consequentially — gave deposed bishops a right of appeal to the bishop of Rome. The library holds six pages of these sentences under PL 8.

Gentian Hervet (1499–1584) — Gentian Hervetus (Hervet), born at Olivet near Orléans in 1499 and died at Reims on 12 September 1584, was a French Catholic theologian, humanist, and controversialist. After studying the humanities at Orléans he went to Paris, where he was tutor to Claude d'Aubespine. Through Thomas Lupset he went to England, where he was charged with the education of a brother of Cardinal Reginald Pole, accompanying his pupil to Rome and remaining some time in Cardinal Pole's house. He later returned to Rome as secretary to Cardinal Cervini (the future Marcellus II), whom he accompanied to the Council of Trent in 1546, where he delivered an oration against clandestine marriages. Ordained priest only in 1556, he became Vicar-General of Noyon and received a canonry at Reims, preaching and writing against the Calvinists. His chief scholarly labor was Latin translation of Greek patristic and canonical texts, including Clement of Alexandria, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Palladius, Nicholas Cabasilas, and the apostolic canons.
b.s: The two pieces held here are conciliar texts tied to Serdica: disciplinary canons on episcopal translation, provincial jurisdiction, and appeals to the Roman see, and a letter rebuking Constantius over Arian interference.

b.bio: No source in this record describes the Hieronymus Romerus who wrote the Explanation of the Chant held here. The biographical surviving records all concern Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus (St. Jerome of Stridon), the Vulgate translator and Latin Father — a different person with a similar name, whose works are not what this library holds under 'Romerus', so none of them may be used for this note. The work itself points to a much later writer: it cites Giovanni Battista Martini, Pius V, and Philip II, and argues about Gothic chant measured in breves and semibreves, so its author belongs to the early modern or eighteenth-century musical-literary world, not late antiquity.
b.s: The single two-page Explanation of the Chant defends a reading of the tones and Gothic mensural notation, attributing Eugenian chant to Saint Eugenius.

b.bio: Heribert Rosweyde was born in Utrecht in January 1569 and died in Antwerp in October 1629. Sources differ on the exact days: Wikipedia gives 20 January and 5 October, while the Dutch Biography Portal gives 22 January and 3 October. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1588 (the Dutch Biography Portal gives 21 May 1588), completed his studies at Douai, and taught philosophy at the Jesuit college there. Searching the monastic libraries of Hainaut and French Flanders, he copied manuscripts of saints' lives and proposed in 1603 to publish them unaltered by later revisers such as Lippomano and Surius. His plan won his superiors' approval but remained unfinished at his death.
b.s: His unfinished project of publishing early hagiographic texts from manuscripts was taken up by Jean Bolland after his death in 1629 and became the Acta Sanctorum, founding the Bollandist enterprise; the works held here are his prefatory letters defending the authenticity and use of martyr records.

w: Letter on the Notes of Fabricius

b.bio: Hermann Samuel Reimarus was born in Hamburg on 22 December 1694 and died there on 1 March 1768. Educated at the Gelehrtenschule des Johanneums and at the University of Jena, he became Privatdozent at Wittenberg in 1716, rector of the high school at Wismar in 1723, and from 1727 until his death taught Hebrew and Oriental languages at the Hamburg Gymnasium. Educated by the scholar J. A. Fabricius, he subsequently became his son-in-law. His posthumously published Apologie oder Schutzschrift für die vernünftigen Verehrer Gottes was issued by Lessing, only in part, as the Wolfenbüttel Fragments; it denied the supernatural origin of Christianity and treated Jesus as a mortal Jewish prophet whose apostles founded a separate religion.
b.s: The single item held here, a Letter on the Notes of Fabricius, reflects his close connection to Johann Albert Fabricius rather than any patristic writing; readers should note that this author is an eighteenth-century Enlightenment critic and Deist, not a Latin Father, despite the shelf heading.

b.bio: Sir Henry Savile was born at Bradley near Halifax, Yorkshire, and educated at Brasenose College before becoming a Fellow of Merton College, Oxford, in 1565. He gained repute as a Greek scholar and mathematician through lectures on Ptolemy's Almagest, served as Greek tutor to Queen Elizabeth, and collected manuscripts on continental travels. He became Warden of Merton in 1585 and Provost of Eton, endowed the Savilian chairs of astronomy and geometry at Oxford, sat in Parliament for Bossiney (1589) and Dunwich (1593), and worked on the King James New Testament translation.
b.s: The library holds only his dedicatory letter (PL 179), which belongs to his role as editor and patron of patristic scholarship rather than as a theological author.

b.bio: Heinrich Leonhard Schurtzfleisch was born in Korbach in Waldeck on 11 November 1664, son of the former court preacher Johann Schurzfleisch. He studied at Wittenberg from 1681 and Jena from 1688, took a doctorate in law at Franeker in 1697, then returned to Wittenberg, where he became adjunct of the philosophical faculty in 1701 and succeeded his brother Konrad Samuel as professor of history in 1702. He served as rector there in 1710, directed the Weimar library from 1708, and became a consistorial councillor in Weimar in 1713. Sources give his death as 1722 or 1723; he was buried in Weimar on 13 July 1722.
b.s: The works held here are his prefatory and dedicatory matter for the Roswitha material in PL 137, in which he defends the identification of Roswitha as a Saxon nun of Gandersheim — distinct from the English abbess Hilda, who died in 680 under Egfrid — against Laurentius Humfredus, Trithemius, Mabillon, Baronius, and Bellarmine, while also defending Otto's deposition of John XII.

b.bio: Jerome the Greek is not Jerome of Stridon, the Latin translator of the Bible; the name invites confusion, but no surviving record describes this Greek author. The work this library holds under this name survives in Migne's Patrologia Graeca 40 and is a Greek theological dialogue in question-and-response form directed against Jewish objectors. It treats the Trinity, the divine persons and eternal generation, baptism, faith, and Scripture, arguing that the Son of God is pre-eternal and uncreated, that divine generation lies beyond human comprehension, and that Scripture itself calls mortal men gods and sons of God. Nothing in the sources establishes dates, place, or office for this Greek author.
b.s: The held work is an apologetic dialogue answering Jewish objections to Christian claims about the Trinity, Christ, and baptism, notable for its method of fitting answers to each questioner.

w: In the chapter on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord

b.bio: Hugh, son of Dalmatius (Dalmace), Count of Semur, and Aremberge of Vergy, was born at Semur-en-Brionnais in Burgundy in 1024. Educated by his grand-uncle Hugh, Bishop of Auxerre, he entered the novitiate at Cluny at fourteen and succeeded Odilo as abbot in 1049. His sixty-year abbacy marked the height of the Cluniac congregation: he founded the first house of Cluniac nuns at Marcigny (1056), served on papal missions to Hungary and Germany, attended councils at Rome (Lateran), Vienne, Plaisance, and Clermont, and stood with Gregory VII against Emperor Henry IV at Canossa. He died at Cluny on 29 April 1109 and was canonized by Callixtus II in 1120.
b.s: As abbot of Cluny from 1049 to 1109 he founded the first Cluniac house of nuns at Marcigny in 1056 and stood with Gregory VII against Emperor Henry IV at Canossa. His letters and statutes present Cluny as an asylum of penitents under Peter and Paul and insist on monastic obedience to the abbot.
